entries.title: The Fatimid Caliphate
entries.summary: The Fatimids were an Ismaili Shia caliphate that ruled from North Africa and later Egypt (909–1171 CE), founding Cairo and rivaling the Abbasids for leadership of the Islamic world.
entries.detailed_information: The Fatimids claimed descent from Fatima and Ali. Rising in Ifriqiya (North Africa), they conquered Egypt in 969 CE and founded Cairo (al-Qahira). They developed a powerful Mediterranean state, promoted Ismaili learning, and built institutions such as al-Azhar (initially as a Fatimid center of learning). Their rule ended when Salahuddin (Saladin) abolished the Fatimid caliphate and restored Abbasid allegiance under Ayyubid authority.
entries.location: North Africa and Egypt; influence in Syria and Hijaz at times
entries.historical_significance: Major Shia caliphate and founder of Cairo as an Islamic capital.
entries.disputed_notes: Fatimid claims and Ismaili doctrines were contested by rival Sunni powers; describe neutrally.
related_questions: How did Salahuddin end Fatimid rule?
